en: Now begins the hymn to the feet of the Veda.
O curved-tusked one of massive body, with a splendor equal to ten million suns!
O God, always grant me freedom from obstacles in all my undertakings.
You who have coiled the king of serpents as an earring and wear the crescent moon as your crest-ornament.
I bow to Duṇḍirāja, who has gathered all great obstacles into a single mass. I salute the Great Mountain, my maternal grandfather, whose own grandfather is the Great Light;
I praise the Cause of the worlds, who is adorned above his neck by the elephant Airāvata.
The sages said:
"O best of sages Jaimini, having reached the city of Puṇḍarīka, what did that great yogi do? You should tell us this as it is new."
Sūta said:
In former times, the wise and venerable Jaimini was in the city of Puṇḍarīka,
which was frequented by great sages, Siddhas, Gandharvas, Yakṣas, and Kinnaras.
In that assembly hall, which was adorned by throngs of dancing celestial nymphs and divine songs,
he beheld the Lord, the Supreme Ishana, dancing.
Seeing him from afar, he prostrated himself like a staff upon the surface of the earth.
Emerging from the omentum, [he beheld] the auspicious nectar of the God’s *tāṇḍava* dance.
Seeing that *tāṇḍava* while looking at the Great Goddess standing by His side,
the sage, his mind filled with great joy, fell prostrate before Him.
Then, having summoned his disciples who had mastered the meaning of the Vedas and the Shastras—
Anikeśa, Makeśa, Satayoga, and Madhava,
as well as Vakranāsa with fuel in hand, Dhūmagandhi, and Kuśāsana— [he spoke].
With these [verses], Jaimini worshipped Mahādeva for the sake of the essential meaning of the Vedas.
Then, by His grace, having grasped the essential meaning of the Vedas and Vedāntas,
he spoke this supreme hymn of Vedānta with palms joined in reverence.
The venerable Jaimini said:
Obeisance to you, O Gaṇapati, Lord of Brahmās, Master of the Veda, who are worshipped by Vighneśa, Vidhi, Mārtaṇḍa, Candra, Indra, and Upendra! || 12 ||

I bow to Kumāra, who wears a forehead-mark honored by the soft lotus-hand of Umā, who has golden earrings and a garland of lotuses. What man is capable of praising Śiva, who is difficult even for Viṣṇu to behold?
Therefore, this praise of me has arisen like a vision of a cloud.
Salutations to Śiva with Ambā; salutations to Śarva, the source of bliss;
salutations to Naṭa, to Rudra, and to the Lord of the Assembly (Sadasaspati).
Salutations to the Lord of Beings, by whose feet the worlds are pierced, by whose crest the shell of the cosmic egg is split asunder, and by whose arms the horizons of the quarters are traversed;
salutations to Him who wears a pair of tinkling anklets and who shines with a garment of skin.
Salutations to the Lord of Creatures, who has the king of serpents as his girdle.
(17) Salutations to the Death of Death, to Soma, to the Yogi, to the wielder of the trident;
salutations to the one adorned with bones, the pure one, the Lord of the worlds. (18)
Salutations to you, the vessel of the entire world and the eye of all the celestial dwellers;
salutations to you, the lord of lineages and the lord of sacred fields.
Salutations to you, O Śaṅkara; let there be salutations to you, O Maṅgala.
Salutations to you, the lord of riches; salutations to the lord of foods.
(20) Salutations to the lord of nourished beings, who rejoices in the eightfold yoga, who grants the desires of his afflicted devotees, and who is praised by those who have offered oblations. (21)
Salutation to the Lord of the five elements, to the Lord of Time;
salutation to the Lord of the Self and to the Lord of the quarters.
Salutation to the Great Lord, the creator of the universe, the sustainer of the universe, who wields the Pināka bow.

Salutations indeed to the one who seizes all, whose eye is Agni, and who possesses the universal form (Viśvarūpa). 23. O Īśāna, salutations to you; O Tatpuruṣa, salutations to you; always salutations to you, the Terrible (Ghora);
salutations to you, O Vāmadeva; and salutations indeed to Sadyojāta. 24.
Salutations to you, Bhava, who are the ornament of prosperity for devotees and are devoted to the destruction of their fear; salutations to Bharga, salutations to Rudra, the bountiful;
salutations to you, O Lord of a thousand, Sāmba, the thousand-limbed one.
To you, the thousand-armed, the thousand-eyed, the bountiful one.

Salutations to you, who have beautiful cheeks, who are like the moon, who have a lovely forehead and beautiful eyebrows, who possess a noble body, who are most gracious, and who are the bountiful giver.
Salutations to you, the invincible, the enduring, the creator.

I bow to him who has beautiful shanks, a slender waist, and strong thighs; who has a beautiful neck and is adorned by the moon; who has handsome cheeks and lovely eyes; who is fragrant and the increaser of prosperity.

I bow to the Lord, the imperishable and supreme Master, whose food is alms, whose garment is green linen, whose ornament is protection, who is patient as the earth, and who is beloved by the Lord of Yakṣas;
he who has half-veiled hair, half-naked, and wears a garland of bones and lotus petals.
I salute the Puruṣa who possesses half the marks of a male, who is dark and tawny;
I bow to that Lord, the master of all that moves and stands, who enables one to cross the great ocean of saṃsāra with a single prostration.
I bow to the protector of the worlds, the Lord, the bestower of all prosperity,
the leader of the Maruts, the unconquered conqueror;
I bow to you, the slayer of Antaka, the bearer of the Mandākinī.
I bow to that Lord, the omniscient, omnipresent, and all-encompassing Seer, who fashioned these three worlds;
from whom the Ṛg-verses, the Yajus-formulas, and the Sāman-chants were born together with their meaning. (35–36)
I bow to you, Sudṛśa, the Lord of the past, the future, and the present—
he who, having abandoned all other activities, beholds the entire universe upon the earth.
I bow with devotion to that supreme Hara, the controller of the gods.
I bow to that Mahādeva by whose command Nārāyaṇa remains pervading the entire universe;
and by whose appointment the Lord Dhātṛ fashioned this world at the beginning of the kalpa, exactly as it was before.
I bow to that Lord,
whose linga the hosts of Maruts, with Indra as their chief, worship day and night together with their wives.
I prostrate before this very Rudra, whom, having worshipped but once in the past, [one attains liberation].
The gods, receiving their portions from Pūṣan, attained their own sovereignty.
I bow to that Lord Īśāna, whom peaceful ascetics, ever perceiving him as Śiva, worship within the lotus of the heart.
Therefore, let us offer praise and salutation to you, the one who possesses the splendor of a lotus.
O Rudra, that auspicious form of yours which has Umā upon its breast and shoulders—to that we bow.
Salutations to you, O Rudra, for your essential being; salutations to you, O Rudra, for your divine play.
Salutations to you, O Rudra, for the sake of peace; salutations to you, O Rudra, in your wrathful aspect.
(44) I bow to Īśāna, who is to be worshipped by all, the bestower of the abundance of prosperity, whose weapon was Hari and whose charioteer was Brahmā. (45)
O Destroyer of Tripura, salutations to you whose feet have crushed horses and chariots,
and salutations to your arms equipped with arrows and bows.
Salutations to the axe, O Lord, to the trident, and to that which possesses the brilliance of fire.
Salutations to you, O Mind, who are the horses, the fires, and the moon; and salutations also to your arrow.
(47) O Śaṅkara, salutations to you, the bowstring of Vāsuki, and to your twanging sound;
salutations be to you, the great one in the form of Mount Meru, and to your bow. (48)
I offer salutations to those other weapons that swiftly snatched away the necklaces of the wives of Suretara and were carried off by Hari;
salutations to them whose arms were struck by the lotus-like play of the daughter of the Mountain-King.
To you we have spoken; homage to him, seeking his aid.
O Nīlalohita, protect me—me who am weak, exhausted, wounded by dice, untrained, helpless, miserable, fallen into calamity, and destitute.
O Lord, protect me, who am foul-mouthed, of evil deeds, and wicked; for among those like me,
I know no protector other than You,
O Śambhu, who consume them with the fire called *bhava*, whose flames are passion, hatred, and pride.
O Compassionate One, be the protector of us who honor the land.
O Purunāman, O Puruṣṭuta, take away my wife of another, my dwelling in another's house, my clothes belonging to another, and that which is displeasing to others; protect me from the food of another!
We endure the insults inflicted by those who are well-nourished and possess many followers.
O Lord of Gods, through your gifts, many beings have become great givers;
O Lord, while the people who have attained this world look on with pride,
provide us with a field, a lifespan, wealth, and likewise sustenance.
O Treasure of Compassion, you alone know our great shame regarding our begging; therefore, quickly bestow [wealth] upon us, your devotees.
May his wife, mother, father, and others not despise us as being witless and destitute. (57)

"Grant me the great Vidyā, O Rādhā, together with Viśvapuṣ. O Merudhanvan, grant strength to my body for all tasks—both those whose results are unseen and those whose results are seen—for I am powerless. (58–59)

O Lord of Gods, destroy the heart-disease and the jaundice of me, who have obtained thousands of enemies and am constantly separated from what is dear. Whatever diseases or piśācas there may be here, [whether affecting] men or gods, [may they not affect] me.
"O God, they all oppress them; subdue them with your great weapon!
You alone are our protector; no other whatsoever exists.
Therefore, O Lord of Gods, O Lord of Prayer (Brahmaṇaspati), take us under your care and protect us!"
O Lord of Umā, you alone are the mother, you are the father, and you are the grandfather;
you are life, you are the intellect, you are prosperity, and you are the supreme brother and friend.
Since you alone, O Lord of Gods, are the agent of every action.
Therefore, forgive all that evil deed which was committed by me.
(64) In sovereignty there is none equal to you, and in insignificance there is none equal to me.
Therefore, O God, O Mahādeva, you are our father. (65)
One should sing of, or contemplate with mind and voice, Him who is firmly established, whose limbs are white as ashes, whose splendor is like the rising sun, whose face is serene, and who is gentle;
for it is He alone who appears to us as You while dancing.
May we behold Umā’s beloved as he surveys the world for a hundred autumns.
(67) Through your grace, may we be free from disease, highly fortunate, wise, and deeply learned; may we live for a hundred autumns. (68)
And may we always drink to our heart's content the nectar of your *tāṇḍava* dance together with our kinsmen; O Īśāna, grant us a hundred autumns!
O God of gods, Mahādeva, [we take refuge in] your lotus-like foot.
"Having drunk the honey-like wine of our desire, may we rejoice for a hundred autumns!
(70) Whether we be insects, serpents, or piśācas—whatever we may be in birth after birth—may we be your servants, O Mahādeva, for a hundred autumns! (71)

O Lord Mahādeva, may we hear for a hundred autumns the divine sounds of dance, music, and song in Your assembly hall with our two ears—sounds that, by mere remembrance, are supreme in destroying the cycle of worldly existence. 72.
Your [powers]... which destroy the cycle of worldly existence through mere remembrance.
We shall proclaim your divine names for a hundred autumns.
O Dhūrjaṭi, who by the mere act of fixing an arrow consumed the three cities, may we remain forever unconquered by mental afflictions and physical diseases for a hundred autumns.
When shall I cause that celebrated young poet— who possesses the luster of beautiful gold, whose feet are like the breasts of Gaurī,
who is surrounded by the lords of the Pramathas, whose face is joyful, and who speaks with affection— to drink [the nectar of my verses]? 75.1–2.

"When shall I serve the radiant Lord accompanied by Ambā, whose splendor is like that of Venus? Will the Blue-throated Lord, the Red-hued One, ever accept me—me who am full of sin, devoid of even a trace of merit, and evil-minded? (76–77)
When will the Lord protect me, whose mind is agitated by the fear of being consumed by the fire of Time?
When will Sugrīva, who bows down before me, protect me?
O singers, come here if you desire Rādhā and the others.
"O friends of the Giver of Wealth, sing this hymn to him in the evening, O men!
Come to me, my friends, if you are seekers of liberation.
Thus praised by the brahmins for the sake of release, he has been lauded. (79–80)
At every step, the footprint of the Lord will surely become moist for us;
one should perform this circumambulation with the eyes fixed on the center.
O two dear friends, every task has indeed been well performed by you both for me.
Join your hands in reverential salutation to Rudra, whose bow is firm.
O four-headed one, bow to Bhava, whose head is above the heads of the Maruts, who bears the crescent moon upon his head, who destroys the head [of the enemy], and whose army is stainless. 82–83.
With eyes that gazed upon a handsome, radiant, golden youth who had subdued the god of love with the arrows born from his own glance,
[he beheld him] in the assembly of the Wielder of the Trident amidst the nectar-like sounds of music for the twilight dance. (84)
Quickly, like two white cows, fall upon the enemy's ears as you desire.
May the two nostrils, which have their chests perfumed by the breath of Vāsuki and whose necks are smeared with poison, grant us well-being as they are smelled.
O friend, Jihvā (the tongue), may there be prosperity for you; [may you be] the bestower of knowledge upon the consort of Umāpati.
Utter a loftier hymn, like the drum of the victorious!
O boat of the mind, do not grieve; perceive the entire world as contemptible.
Pārvatī is not thirsty; drink the nectar of Śambhu’s dance.
Fragrant, pleasant to the touch, granting desires, and adorned by the moon—
embrace me firmly with your heart, O woman, as a lover embraces his beloved.
To him of great rays, great arms, great body, and great garments.
I offer this well-composed hymn of praise to the Great Diadem-wearer, the Great Lord, the Most Exalted.
(90) In whatever way we have fashioned these beautiful hymns with devotion through the grace of the Lord, let us most certainly worship Maheśa, the Subduer, with them. (91)
Salutations to Śiva, the destroyer of Tripura, the Lord of the three worlds, the one clad in space.
Salutations be to the foremost Hara; again, salutations to the lowest and to the one who dwells at the base.
Salutations to you, the transformation and the transformer; salutations be to Bhava and to the source of existence.
To Him from whom the progenitor of the world was born, who possesses many forms of diverse appearances at the end of creation—
to that Supreme One, whose golden throne is covered with various jewels from the crowns of the lords of gods,
who has ashes as His body-unguent, and than whom nothing higher exists, I offer salutation. (93–94)
Salutations to you, whose matted locks form a thicket agitated by the battle between the king of serpents and the lord of medicinal herbs;
salutations to you whose beautiful *tāṇḍava* dance contains within it the entire universe.
I eternally bow to this enemy of Tripura, the end-maker of Yama, the father of the six-faced one, and the Lord.
I bow with reverence to that ancient God who exists beyond darkness, whose flower-bow was afflicted by the eye on his forehead;
who has his lotus-feet sought after by the eyes of Murāri; whose hands are stained by the lac-dye from Umā’s feet; who has a throat dark blue like poison, golden tusks, and a pure complexion. (96–97)

I bow to that which is infinite, unmanifest, inconceivable, one, the destroyer, whose garment is the sky, who resembles the sky, unborn, ancient, who is subtler than the subtle and greater than the great— He who dwells within. Failing to perceive the unborn Self dwelling within, the deluded wander in error through mountain caves.

Was he behind? Was he to the south? Was he in front? Was he below? Or was he above? (99) I bow to this Lord, the moon-crested Śiva, the Great Bliss, who is free from sorrow and suffering—he who dwells within the lotus of the heart, having encompassed all the intermediate and cardinal directions. (100)

Beholding me shattered by the great disease called worldly existence, which arises from unwholesome conditions such as passion and the like, protect me, O Moon-crested One; for I hear that you are the best of physicians among all beings.
[101] Behold me, who am an ocean of suffering devoid of even a trace of happiness, untouched by merit, and burdened with many sins.
We, who are terrified of the serpent of worldly existence and held in the very hand of Death from behind, before, below, and above—

may we quickly cross over these misfortunes by means of that glance, which is like a beautiful song from the lovely face of the Daughter of the Mountain King, and which is itself full of compassion. || 102 ||

O Maheśa, protect me, who am sinking in the midst of the shoreless ocean of saṃsāra and crying out with no small passion; grant me an inexhaustible gift through your most powerful and gracious favor. 104
O Enemy of Yama, remembering my previously accumulated sins as I stand before the fierce Yama, I am afraid;
grant me whatever lifespan I desire, whether it be a short life or even death.
[With] infinite, soft, and non-terrible coils, white with beautiful fragrant ashes—
When will the wielder of the Pināka bow, the fierce one of many forms, embrace me with his firm arms?
When will the Lord, the God of gods, who is golden-hued and golden-eyed, protect me as I cry out, fallen into the ocean of existence like an extremely terrified frog in the mouth of a serpent?

"When shall I behold that God, who possesses a beautiful smile, who is adorned with a digit of the moon, whose single eye is worthy of Gaurī’s sidelong glances, and who, radiant as the sun, stands beyond all darkness?
O you who desire liberation, come here quickly, you who meditate upon Śiva within the lotus of your heart. (108)
For those who have ascertained the meaning through the realization of Vedānta meditate upon this [Lord] constantly for the sake of liberation.
(109) "Come, you who desire sovereignty over the world; worship Maheśa but once!
Having worshipped him in the past, Hiraṇyagarbha became the sole lord of all that has come into being. (110)
May those who desire vast prosperity worship this Śrīkaṇṭha even once;
for he is the illustrious Lord of Śrī, whose feet are worshipped by the Lord of Śrī himself, the noble sustainer of fortunes and the source of riches.
May even those men who long for virtuous sons worship this youthful Giriśa.
From whom the self-existent Hiraṇyagarbha, the creator of the worlds, came into being in the beginning.
(112) What is the use of many words that have not been spoken? Everything is accomplished by taking refuge in him.
For in former times, having taken refuge in him, the pot-born Agastya—who was not able to drink up the ocean—became young again despite his grey hair. (113)
Abandoning all others, O bees that are my eyes, always take refuge in this auspicious one;
for he is fragrant, gentle, and auspicious, and indeed he is sweet and full of honey.
You shall become devoid of a counterpart, having utterly conquered all men and gods;
homage be to you, O Vāṇī! Praise this Great Lord, the youthful Śrutagartanada.
Whatever you desire in your mind, all that shall surely come to pass for you.
When suffering has ceased regarding this matter, we shall at some point offer worship to Rudra for our well-being.
Whatever act of transgression was previously committed by us through the power of ignorance toward you—
Therefore, O Compassionate One, having drunk all this, please favor us as if toward your own sons.

(117) The compassionate Lord Śiva, the wielder of the Pināka bow, became my protector when I was bitten by the fierce fangs of passion, hatred, madness, greed, and the like— the serpents of this world known as *saṃsāra*— and he granted me the remedy of his glance.
Having spoken thus at the conclusion of his meditative absorption, the practitioner of mantra, having meditated upon Rudra, departs—just as those bitten by the serpent of worldly birth do.
Being virtuous, I approach with reverence through the Brahman, by means of the essence of the Nīlagrīva mantra.

O Lord of the helpless, touch with Your healing hand those who are afflicted by the most terrifying fever of worldly existence, who are beset by great fear, who are the abode of all sins, and whose time of death is near; O Hero, touch them for the sake of our prosperity. May we conquer all this that is desired—this entire earth, the regions of the eight directions, the realm of the sky, and the realm of heaven, along with everything contained therein.

Homage to you, Bhava; homage to Hara, who is resplendent with majesty; homage to the one who delights in the world, the destroyer of the fear and affliction of worldly existence. Homage to Śiva, the protector of the universe, the eternal wielder of the trident, whose friend is never slain and who is never conquered at any time. He who bestows upon all the gods and dānavas wealth that is firmly established in a golden hue—[to him] I offer this hymn. (121) Homage to Bhava, to Hara, who is illumined by his own power; homage to the one who removes worldly existence, the dispeller of the terror of the suffering of saṃsāra.
Homage to Śiva, the protector of the world, the eternal, the bearer of the trident, whose companion is never struck down and who is never defeated at any time. (121)
Homage, homage to the Lord of the gods; homage, homage to the Lord of the lords of the earth;
homage, homage to the Lord of the bowstring (Śiva); homage, homage to the Lord of Ambikā, the Lord of Umā, the Lord of Creatures—homage, homage!

I bow eternally to Vināyaka, who destroys the suffering of those who prostrate before him; he whose entire body is marked by the sound of the slapping of his hands upon his head and the touch of his thumbs, the poet among poets, possessed of most excellent fame.
(124) The gods in battle and the brahmins at sacrifice [attain] their own success, again and again.
I bow to Skanda, who grants success; I bow to Subrahmaṇya, the fierce Subrahmaṇya. (125) Homage to Śivā, the Mother of the World, the beloved of Śiva, whose very form is auspiciousness.
She emerged as the daughter of the Lord of Mountains, a youth of exquisite beauty who bestows the four goals of life. (126)

I bow to Gaurī, who is golden-hued, whose feet are adorned with jeweled anklets, whose face is serene, who holds a lotus in her hand and a silken garment, whose eyes are wide, who knows all speech, and who utters sacred words.
I pay homage to this immeasurable Umā, the daughter of Menā, who is full of grace and worthy of honor.
She who, embracing her dear friend, makes her two breasts appear as if covered in frost;

this beloved goddess Umā, whose splendor is exceedingly lovely, who wanders about, and before whom the lord of monkeys bows—she stands at the side of Giriśa, the goddess beholding all the worlds. (128–129)
I bow to Gaurī, whose breasts are high and full, who wears the crescent moon as her crest-ornament, and whose every limb is anointed with pure unguents;

this Goddess, the inner self of all living beings, impels every god toward the granting of boons. I bow to her, whose delight is the protection of the wretched, and to this maiden who bestows joy upon those who are bowed in devotion.
She who is the leader of all sciences, of auspicious things, and of words—of wealth, grace, and truth;

she who destroys both worldly existence and its opposite, and who enjoys the ornaments of the portion of worldly existence—O beloved of Śiva, grant me that supreme intellect by which we may cross over all misfortunes. 131–132.

O Śivā, how can you be praised with hymns when this Śiva, the Lord who sports in the three worlds, is your husband; while Hari is but a servant, as are his followers Indira, Śacī, Sarasvatī, the fortunate Aditi, and Vasu?
The best of the twice-born who recites this hymn composed by Jaimini with devotion to the Lord [attains the highest state].
The goddesses of desired speech, accomplishment, intellect, and fortune embrace him as they would a son according to their own inclination.

(134) Furthermore, the enemy kings who desire to fight, if they recite this with devotion, will quickly depart with equal devotion; or else, harboring extreme fear in their hearts, the enemies shall swiftly go to the God of Death. (135)
Those desiring intelligence obtain wisdom by reciting this; likewise, those desiring long life obtain longevity.
Similarly, those desiring prosperity obtain fortune, and they indeed obtain sons and grandsons.
(136) Thus ends the *Vedapādastava* composed by the great sage Śrī Jaimini.
